title: Throwing a soap dish with drainage ribs
subtitle: A shallow thrown stoneware dish with three raised clay ribs that lift a bar of soap clear of standing water
excerpt: A soap dish with raised drainage ribs solves a practical problem: a bar of soap sitting in a puddle dissolves faster and goes slimy. The ribs are three thin clay ridges applied to the interior of the dish at the leather-hard stage, raising the soap bar a few millimetres so water drains freely beneath it. The dish itself is a shallow thrown form, straightforward at beginner level, with the rib attachment as a small extra step.
sourceNotes: Soap dish throwing pattern derived from first principles. Drainage rib application technique is a traditional studio practice; no single primary source. V&A open-access collection for utilitarian bathroom ceramics reference.

glossaryTerms.definition: The working stage where clay holds its shape but remains damp enough to join and attach clay additions
Air-dried but unfired; fragile, ready for bisque firing
The trimmed ridge at the base that the dish sits on, keeping the base level
The first firing, around cone 06 (1000 degrees Celsius), that hardens greenware into porous bisqueware
Scratching the clay surface and applying water or liquid clay before joining two pieces, to ensure a strong mechanical bond

content.text: A thrown soap dish is a small, practical piece that introduces beginners to shallow open forms: a dish roughly 12 cm wide, 8 cm long in profile, and only 3 cm deep, with a slightly curved interior base. Three narrow clay ribs, applied to the floor of the dish at the
leather-hard
stage by the
score and slip
method, keep the soap bar elevated. Water drains under the ribs and the soap stays dry between uses.
Shallow throwing is its own skill. The clay opens wide fast and the walls are short. Off-centre throwing shows right away. Centre with care. Open slowly. Stop as soon as the dish shape is done.

attrs.title: Studio safety
attrs.content: Silica dust is the chronic studio hazard. Silicosis is irreversible. Mix wet whenever possible. Wear a P100 respirator any time raw glaze powders are open. Wet-clean only: no sweeping, no compressed air, no dry sanding indoors. Ventilation matters: a downdraft vent or open window with an extractor. Wear welder's shade-5 glasses when peephole-watching at high temperatures. Never open a hot kiln below 80 degrees Celsius. Keep a Class A fire extinguisher within reach.

content.text: What you'll need

materials.name: Smooth stoneware clay
materials.quantity: 300 g for dish plus 50 g for ribs

materials.name: Mid-fire glaze, pre-mixed
materials.quantity: small amount for one soap dish

content.text: Preparation

Wedge 300 g of smooth stoneware for the dish and set aside a small 50 g piece wrapped in plastic for the drainage ribs. The ribs will be rolled from this small piece at the leather-hard stage, so keep it wrapped to prevent it drying out during throwing. Fix a bat to the wheel head. A bat is useful here because a wide, shallow dish is awkward to wire off and lift without distorting the thin walls.
Throwing the dish
Centre 300 g of stoneware on the bat at medium speed. Centre thoroughly: a shallow dish amplifies any off-centre throwing into a visible wobble at the rim.

Open the floor slowly. Press two fingers into the centre and draw outward to a floor diameter of 90 mm, leaving 6 mm at the base. For a soap dish, the floor width at this stage is almost the finished interior width.

Pull the low walls upward in one pass: the walls only need to rise 30 to 35 mm. Keep them at 5 to 6 mm thick. A shallow dish with thick walls looks clumsy, but too thin a wall will be fragile and prone to chipping at the rim.

With the wooden rib held flat against the interior floor, smooth the floor in a single pass from the centre outward as the wheel turns slowly. This both smooths and slightly compresses the base, which helps prevent cracking as the dish dries.

Smooth the rim with the chamois leather. Level any uneven sections with the needle tool. The dish rim should be at a consistent height all around: 30 to 35 mm from the bat surface. Wire off and leave on the bat to dry to
leather-hard
before adding the ribs.
Attaching the drainage ribs
When the dish has reached leather-hard, unwrap the reserved 50 g piece of clay. Roll three short coils on a clean surface, each about 80 mm long and 6 to 7 mm in diameter. Taper each end slightly.
Mark three parallel lines on the interior floor of the dish with the needle tool, evenly spaced about 20 mm apart and running the length of the dish interior. These are the attachment lines.
Score and slip
: scratch the marked lines with the needle tool to roughen the surface, then wet each line with a dab of water.

Press each clay coil onto a scored line. The coil should stand upright as a raised rib, not lie flat. Press both ends of each rib firmly down onto the scored surface and smooth the join with a moistened fingertip.
Check that all three ribs are the same height: approximately 5 to 6 mm above the dish floor. Place your bar of soap across all three ribs to test that it sits level and stable.
Trimming
Once the ribs have stiffened and joined firmly (give it an extra hour after attaching), invert the dish on the wheel and trim a shallow
foot ring
using the loop tool: 4 mm tall, at a diameter of 70 mm. The foot ring keeps the base flat and prevents the dish rocking on an uneven surface.
Smooth the foot ring edges with a damp finger. Return the dish right-side up and let it continue drying.
Drying
Dry the dish right-side up on a wire rack to
bone-dry

. The ribs may dry faster than the dish floor because they have more exposed surface area: cover the interior of the dish loosely with plastic for the first 12 hours to even out drying rates. The rib joins are the most vulnerable point; any cracking at the joins indicates that the ribs and dish dried at too different a rate.
Bisque firing
Load the bone-dry dish upright (ribs uppermost) on a kiln shelf.
Bisque

fire to cone 06 (1000 degrees Celsius). Use a slow ramp: 60 degrees Celsius per hour to 120 degrees Celsius, then 100 degrees Celsius per hour to cone 06. Hold 10 minutes at peak. Cool fully before opening the kiln.
Glazing and glaze firing

Dip-glaze the exterior and interior in one pass, or brush two coats onto the interior (including the ribs) and exterior. Leave the foot ring and base clear. Wipe the foot ring clean with a damp sponge. For a bathroom context, a pale matte or satin glaze in a neutral colour suits the piece well. Glaze-fire to cone 6 (1220 degrees Celsius).
Care

Cone 6 stoneware is non-porous after firing and safe in contact with soap and water. The dish is dishwasher-safe. The drainage ribs are fixed and fire-permanent: they will not detach in normal use. If soap residue builds up between the ribs, rinse with warm water or soak briefly and brush gently with a soft toothbrush.
Variations

Rather than straight ribs, roll three tapered ridges and curve each one slightly before pressing into place. The gentle curve adds visual interest and drains water toward the lower end of the dish if the dish is placed on a sloped surface near the sink.
A sponge holder uses the same form. Make the interior 15 cm wide and use four ribs spaced further apart. It holds a kitchen sponge upright at the sink instead of a soap bar.

rows.problem: Drainage ribs crack at the joins after drying
rows.cause: The ribs and the dish floor were at different moisture levels when joined, or the score-and-slip was not thorough enough
rows.fix: Join the ribs when dish and rib clay are at identical leather-hard stage. Score deeply with the needle tool and wet the scored surface before pressing the rib down firmly.

rows.problem: Soap bar rocks on the ribs rather than sitting level
rows.cause: Ribs not aligned parallel to each other or at different heights
rows.fix: Use a ruler to mark the rib positions before scoring. Test the bar of soap across all three ribs before the clay stiffens and adjust rib height by pressing down any rib that is too tall.

rows.problem: Dish floor bows upward in the centre after firing
rows.cause: Base was not compressed enough during throwing
rows.fix: After opening, spend one extra pass compressing the base floor with the wooden rib held flat. A well-compressed base shrinks evenly during firing.

rows.problem: Glaze runs off the ribs and thins to bare clay after firing
rows.cause: Glaze coat too thin on the narrow rib surfaces
rows.fix: Apply one extra brush coat to the ribs specifically before loading. The narrow profile of the ribs sheds glaze faster than the flat floor during dipping.
